correctness.rationale: For N/2<ell<=N the direct existential-removal definition reduces to prefix-balance. Top ell goods must occupy all ell agents bijectively, and each of the remaining N-ell goods must match injectively with a top good of its own multipartite class, giving the exact falling-factorial count and feasibility iff 2x_i<=n_i. Hypergeometric sampling over bottom sets gives the probability coefficient. The normal limit uses the correct mean, variance and finite-population CLT; Chebyshev handles larger surpluses. A separately implemented direct definition and exhaustive small-case allocations match the theorem. The worst-case threshold uses cited earlier strong-colorability monotonicity, not empirical extrapolation.

originality.rationale: Direct full-text comparison with Haviv (2026) distinguishes his universal SD-EF1 existence and balanced bipartite strong-colorability threshold from the presently proved complete allocation-count distribution and the random-order Gaussian transition. Equbal et al. (2026) focus on incomplete EF1/maximality, and Hummel--Hetland (2021) on EF1/MMS conflicting items. Targeted published research-record searches yielded only distinct stochastic assignment and graph-coloring questions. Known general hypergeometric CLT and Haviv prefix lemma are acknowledged as ingredients; an unindexed identical computation remains possible.
residual_risks: Unindexed equivalent enumerations and implicit deductions in adjacent strong-coloring work could exist.

The counting formula follows a short argument using Haviv's existing ranked-block insight; its significance rests on the exact probability and sharp random-versus-worst-case Gaussian transition, not on complexity of the finite counting argument.

value.rationale: The exact success probability is a natural service-reliability metric when items have a random common priority order; it measures an unknown intermediate regime left unresolved by a worst-case-only existence criterion. The critical window proves a structurally meaningful separation: m+Theta(sqrt(m)) agents suffice for a nonzero or high typical success rate while the adversarial threshold is ceil(3m/2). The all-size enumerative law and Gaussian scaling are exact, not arbitrary small-instance tables, and can inform prioritization and agent-capacity planning. The known balanced worst-case threshold is not counted as an original contribution.
